anchor.title: Family newly arrived in Chicago from the South
anchor.creator: Chicago Commission on Race Relations
anchor.citation: Chicago Commission on Race Relations. "Family Newly Arrived from the South." The Negro in Chicago: A Study of Race Relations and a Race Riot. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1922. https://archive.org/details/negroinchicagost00chic.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of an African American family of nine adults and children, dressed in winter coats and hats, standing together with suitcases and bundled belongings at their feet, having recently arrived in Chicago, c. 1920.
anchor.caption: An African American family of nine, dressed in coats and hats with their suitcases at their feet, photographed shortly after arriving in Chicago during the Great Migration, when hundreds of thousands of Black Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities. It illustrates Tennessee standard US.28 on the Great Migration.

anchor.title: The "Spirit of St. Louis," Col. Lindbergh's plane
anchor.creator: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
anchor.citation: "The Spirit of St. Louis, Col. Lindbergh's Famous Plane." Photograph. 1927. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/item/92520351/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of the single-engine monoplane "Spirit of St. Louis" on the ground in 1927, with a small group of people gathered beside it.
anchor.caption: Charles Lindbergh's monoplane the "Spirit of St. Louis," which he flew solo across the Atlantic Ocean in May 1927. Lindbergh became an instant celebrity, his feat broadcast by radio and newsreel to a mass audience, illustrating Tennessee standards US.29 (mass culture and celebrity) and US.31 (new air travel).

anchor.title: Bessie Smith, "Empress of the Blues"
anchor.creator: Carl Van Vechten / Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
anchor.citation: "Bessie Smith." Photograph. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/item/2004663577/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white studio portrait of Bessie Smith, an African American woman in a beaded dress, posed in front of a draped backdrop.
anchor.caption: Portrait of Bessie Smith, the African American blues singer known as the "Empress of the Blues," whose recordings sold millions in the 1920s and helped bring blues music into the cultural mainstream. It illustrates Tennessee standard US.30 on the rise of blues music.

anchor.title: Ford Motor Company moving assembly line
anchor.creator: Ford Motor Company
anchor.citation: "Ford Assembly Line, 1913." Photograph. Ford Motor Company, 1913. Wikimedia Commons. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ford_assembly_line_-_1913.jpg.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph of workers lined along the Ford moving assembly line in 1913, with automobile chassis advancing along a long industrial factory line.
anchor.caption: Workers along the Ford Motor Company moving assembly line in 1913, where automobiles moved past stationary workers who each performed a single task. This mass-production method made the Model T affordable and transformed American industry, illustrating Tennessee standard US.32 on Henry Ford and mass production.

anchor.title: Louis Armstrong
anchor.creator: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
anchor.citation: "Louis Armstrong." Photograph. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/item/97518323/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white portrait of Louis Armstrong, an African American man holding a white handkerchief, in a light suit.
anchor.caption: Portrait of Louis Armstrong, the African American jazz trumpeter and singer whose virtuosic playing helped define the Jazz Age and the Harlem Renaissance. It illustrates Tennessee standard US.33 on the Harlem Renaissance.

anchor.title: A flapper girl
anchor.creator: Turner, C. W., photographer
anchor.citation: Turner, C. W., photographer. A flapper girl. c1922. Photographic print. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C., SSF - Clothing and Dress -- 1922 [item] [P&P], LC-USZ62-38343. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2012645724/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: A young woman stands confidently outdoors in winter, dressed in a long fashionable coat with a luxurious fur collar framing her face, a close-fitting cap, and sturdy boots. Her pose and attire reflect 1920s flapper style with poised modernity.
anchor.caption: This 1922 photograph captures a flapper girl in stylish winter attire, embodying the Jazz Age's bold cultural shift toward women's fashion and social freedoms that defined the Roaring Twenties.

anchor.title: Ku Klux Klan parade, Washington, D.C.
anchor.creator: National Photo Company / Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
anchor.citation: "Ku Klux Klan Parade, Washington, D.C." Photograph. September 13, 1926. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/item/93513529/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph showing a long mass parade of robed Ku Klux Klan members marching down a wide Washington, D.C. avenue lined with buildings and crowds, 1926.
anchor.caption: Robed Ku Klux Klan members marching in a mass parade down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., on September 13, 1926. The 1920s saw a nationwide resurgence of the Klan, which targeted African Americans, immigrants, Catholics, and Jews, illustrating Tennessee standard US.35 on racial and ethnic tensions.

anchor.title: Clarence Darrow at the Scopes Trial, Dayton, Tennessee
anchor.creator: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division
anchor.citation: "Clarence Darrow." Photograph. 1925. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/item/2005687216/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: Black-and-white portrait of attorney Clarence Darrow, an older man in a suit, photographed around the time of the 1925 Scopes Trial.
anchor.caption: Attorney Clarence Darrow, who defended teacher John Scopes at the 1925 Scopes "Monkey" Trial in Dayton, Tennessee, where the teaching of evolution was put on trial. It illustrates Tennessee standard US.36 on the Scopes Trial.

anchor.title: A camel got his head in, and then -- !
anchor.creator: Pease, Lute, 1869-1963, artist
anchor.citation: Pease, Lute. "A camel got his head in, and then -- !" Drawing. Between 1917 and 1920. Cartoon Drawings (Library of Congress). Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, Washington, D.C. https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/2016683882/.
anchor.rights: Public Domain — No Known Restrictions on Publication
anchor.alt: A large camel pushes its head and front through the flap of a tent labeled 'U.S.', its body outside. Inside, a disheveled man in shirtsleeves labeled 'Wets' recoils in dismay, arms raised. The title 'A camel got his head in, and then -- !' appears above, with the camel's hump labeled 'National Prohibition Amendment'. Black ink drawing on white background. (62 words)
anchor.caption: This 1919 political cartoon depicts a camel labeled 'National Prohibition Amendment' forcing its way into a U.S. tent, pushing out a 'Wets' opponent, symbolizing the unstoppable ratification of the 18th Amendment banning alcohol. It highlights Tennessee standard US.37 on Prohibition's constitutional impact.
